html:
An act of the English Parliament of December 1689 that set limits on the power of the crown and laid down rights of Parliament. It came out of the Glorious Revolution of 1688, when the Catholic king James II fled and his Protestant daughter Mary and her Dutch husband William of Orange took the throne as William III and Mary II.

Among other things, it said that the monarch could not:

  • suspend laws or raise taxes without Parliament's consent;
  • keep a standing army in peacetime without that consent;
  • interfere with free elections or free speech in Parliament.

It also gave subjects the right to petition the king, banned cruel and unusual punishments, and barred Catholics from the throne.

The act did not create democracy, but it moved power for good from the crown to Parliament and is a founding text of constitutional monarchy in Britain. Parliament's new control of money helped create the Bank of England in 1694. Its wording echoes a century later in the United States Bill of Rights.
